clue.text: Try to deceive dozy charwoman with fake pewter

indicators.note: a dozy worker is muddled and confused, so the letters of the cleaner's title are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: fake metal is counterfeit, a reworked version, so these letters of the alloy are also rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sleepy cleaning lady is fobbed off with imitation tableware.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagram signals, 'dozy' and 'fake', work together: the letters of CHARWOMAN and PEWTER are pooled and rearranged into the fifteen-letter phrase. It is Australian slang.
explanation.definitionFit: An Australian idiom meaning to attempt a deception or try to put one over on somebody.

clue.text: "There was no better bespoke tailor"

parts.note: reads as an epitaph praising a tailor, and a tailor's best praise is that his clothes sat perfectly on the customer

explanation.surface: An obituary line praising a departed tailor of made-to-measure suits.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is normally a tribute paid in someone's honour; here a tailor's 'tribute' is literally a good fit, the quality he was famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted words are a suitably worded epitaph, the kind of eulogy that suits a tailor because tailors are judged on fit.

clue.text: The wit of Christmas, the 7 of 7?

parts.note: Noel is French-derived word for Christmas, used in carols
the second word of 7-down, a chicken in slang, means a coward

explanation.surface: Who was the funniest man of the festive season, and what was the seventh of something?
explanation.walkthrough: 'the 7 of 7' sends you to 7-down, HEADLESS CHICKEN; its seventh-letter word, CHICKEN, is slang for a coward. The playwright Noël Coward was famous for his wit.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright and songwriter Noël Coward was celebrated for his epigrams, a byword for urbane wit.

clue.text: Mine host not so tipsy?

definitions.meaning: an old jocular term for an innkeeper; an archaic word for one who keeps an inn with stables
tipsy as in unsteady, so less wobbly is more steady

explanation.surface: Is the landlord less drunk than his customers?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine host' looks like the landlord himself; it is defined by an archaic word for an innkeeper keeping stables. 'Tipsy' also means likely to tip over, so 'not so tipsy' is a comparative of steady.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is an archaic name for an innkeeper or keeper of a livery stable; the other is the comparative of steady.

clue.text: Indigestion, say, caused by French bread

definitions.meaning: indigestion is an example of discomfort or ache

explanation.surface: Stomach ache brought on by eating baguettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigestion is one kind of physical suffering, and the French for loaf or bread is spelt the same way.

clue.text: If Whitehall sent out penalties now … ?

indicators.note: sent out suggests the letters are dispatched and scattered, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Government officials hand out fines, a speculation about what Whitehall might do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges IF WHITEHALL SENT. The definition is indirect: in a drawn cup tie, the end of normal play means a penalty shoot-out comes now. 'Whitehall' is the street of UK government offices.
explanation.definitionFit: When the referee ends a drawn knockout match, the next thing to follow is a penalty shoot-out, so that signal means spot kicks are imminent.

clue.text: Raven going spare?

parts.note: a cowardly word for chicken with its head removed leaves the name of a black bird, and losing your head is going spare

explanation.surface: A black bird of the crow family is flapping about in a fury.
explanation.walkthrough: Craven means cowardly, i.e. chicken; take its head off and you get RAVEN. 'Going spare' is British slang for frantic, which is how a headless chicken behaves.
explanation.definitionFit: To run about like a headless chicken is to panic frantically, which matches the British idiom for being beside oneself.

clue.text: Face conservative at conference venue?

parts.note: British party conferences are traditionally held in seaside towns, so they are on the sea front

explanation.surface: A Tory meets someone head-on at the party conference.
explanation.walkthrough: UK party conferences are usually held at seaside resorts such as Blackpool or Brighton, on the promenade or sea front.
explanation.definitionFit: To face someone is to stand up to or meet them head-on, a direct synonym.

clue.text: (Wo)man he lays out

indicators.note: laying things out spreads them in a new arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man spreads things out.
explanation.walkthrough: '(Wo)man' shows that the forename is given to both sexes, like Ashley Cole and Ashley Judd.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a first name used for both boys and girls, so it can denote a man or a woman.

clue.text: Some food nite out during the fifties

indicators.note: during places one thing in the midst of another, so the jumbled letters sit within

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so two fifties give LL

indicators.note: a night out is a wild one, signalling these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something to eat on a night out back in the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nite' is a casual spelling of night, and 'the fifties' looks like a decade but is two Roman numerals; 'out' and 'during' are the signals.
explanation.definitionFit: A lentil is a small edible pulse, an example of food.

clue.text: The real McCoy in a bed of feathers?

indicators.note: to feather an oar is to turn it flat, so feathers signals turning the letters into new order

explanation.surface: Something genuine nestling in a feather mattress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feathers' is an unusual anagram signal: feathering an oar means turning its blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for in good faith, it describes something genuine, which is what the idiom the real McCoy means.

clue.text: Hit a crook from Bangkok

indicators.note: a crook is a bend, as in the crook of the arm, so the letters are bent out of order

explanation.surface: A villain from the Thai capital strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a criminal noun; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something from Bangkok comes from Thailand, so the adjective of that nation fits.

clue.text: Vacuous? Waiting for confirmation

definitions.meaning: jokingly, an empty head is a mind left wide open
not yet decided, receptive to evidence before judging

explanation.surface: Someone empty-headed or someone reserving judgment.
explanation.definitionFit: Being receptive to new ideas means withholding judgment until proof arrives; facetiously, an empty mind is unclosed.

clue.text: Capital Radio's Mike recorded after hospital discharge

parts.note: Mike is the radio alphabet code word for M

indicators.note: discharge means sent out, so the hospital letter is let go

parts.note: something filmed and stored is on the video

explanation.surface: A DJ from a London radio station tapes something after leaving hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital Radio' is a London station, but 'Capital' is the definition. 'after hospital discharge' takes H from ON THE VIDEO.
explanation.definitionFit: Montevideo is the capital city of Uruguay.

clue.text: M, le swimmer?

parts.note: M stands for Monsieur, so a Frenchman who swims is pictured; slang for French plus man

explanation.surface: A French gentleman titled Monsieur Swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: M. is the abbreviation for Monsieur; a Frenchman is jokily a 'frog' in British slang, so a French man swimming suggests the underwater diver.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver who swims underwater with flippers and breathing apparatus, pictured here as a swimming Frenchman.

clue.text: Some of us earthlings don't need art nouveau!

indicators.note: do without, so these letters are dropped from the pool
French for new, signalling the remaining letters are made new by rearrangement

explanation.surface: People on Earth can do without Art Nouveau decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some of us' looks like it signals a hidden word; it is the definition, a nation. EARTHLINGS minus A, R, T leaves EHLINGS, which 'nouveau' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A nationality is a group within humanity, so the people of England are some of us.

clue.text: Shy, wearing GP's beard?

parts.note: if you are wearing something you are in it
a general practitioner is a doctor, abbreviated DR
an awn is the bristly beard on an ear of barley or other grass

explanation.surface: A timid person dressed in a family doctor's beard.
explanation.definitionFit: Indrawn means reserved and introverted, a synonym for timid.

clue.text: Steps pointedly taken to rewrite "Coward's End"

indicators.note: rewriting a title puts its letters into a new form

explanation.surface: A dance number added to a rewritten Coward play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward's End' looks like Noël Coward from 3-down, but it is just the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps danced over crossed blades, so pointed metal is involved; a playful description of the Highland dance.

clue.text: That's lovely, so lovely! Turning over, I won't interrupt the view

indicators.note: turning something over reverses it, so the run is read from the end

parts.note: ah is a sigh of delight
a second ah of delight

explanation.surface: Someone delighting in a pleasant landscape, promising not to spoil it.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunken ditch-and-wall boundary in English country estates that keeps livestock out without blocking the view.
explanation.definitionFit: The sunken fence is designed precisely so the landscape stays unbroken, here speaking in the first person.

clue.text: Who every so often drops skilful footballer?

definitions.meaning: one who lets liquid fall drop by drop, like a baby
a player who runs with the ball under close control past opponents

explanation.surface: Who is it that periodically gets dropped from the team, a gifted footballer?
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is someone who lets saliva fall in drips; the other is a soccer player good at running with the ball.

clue.text: It's a sign of the Welsh League, I'm afraid!

parts.note: eek is a cry of fright

explanation.surface: A grim admission about the state of Welsh league football.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm afraid' reads as an apologetic aside but is a cry of fear.
explanation.definitionFit: The vegetable is a national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day.

clue.text: Creature practising extremist religion?

parts.note: to be practising a faith is to be in it
a sect is a breakaway, often extreme, religious group

explanation.surface: A being who follows a fringe religion.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect is a small six-legged creature, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Wrapping up what's electronic

indicators.note: stirred or mixed up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: Asking what counts as electronic when finishing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrapping up' looks like one phrase meaning concluding; 'Wrapping' is the definition and 'up' the anagram signal on WHAT'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A swathe is a band of cloth or bandage used to wrap something.

clue.text: At sea directors who don't eat quiche, as a TV host would say?

indicators.text: as a TV host would say
indicators.note: Jonathan Ross, the TV presenter, famously pronounces R as W, so the phrase is spoken his way

parts.note: from the book title claiming real men don't eat quiche

explanation.surface: Ship's officers who avoid quiche, in a chat-show host's phrasing.
explanation.walkthrough: Real Men Don't Eat Quiche was a 1982 humour bestseller. Spoken with Jonathan Ross's R-as-W, 'real men' becomes 'weal men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Helmsmen steer, or direct, a ship at sea from the wheel.
